sessions.author: Priya
sessions.content: For sorted arrays, put one pointer at each end. If the sum is too big, move the right pointer left; too small, move the left pointer right. You never need a nested loop because every move throws away a whole set of impossible pairs.

sessions.author: Aman
sessions.content: I keep getting off-by-one errors in binary search. Sometimes my loop runs forever when lo=mid. When do I use lo<=hi versus lo<hi?

sessions.author: Rahul
sessions.content: Pick an invariant and stick to it: the answer is always inside [lo, hi]. If you use lo<=hi, shrink with mid+1 and mid-1. If you use lo<hi, one side must be mid, and you must round mid up when you move lo. The infinite loop happens when mid rounds down and lo=mid.

sessions.author: Priya
sessions.content: Treat a hash map as a notebook that answers 'have I seen this before?' in constant time. For two-sum, store each number as you go and check whether target minus current is already in the notebook.

sessions.author: Rahul
sessions.content: Trust the recursive call. Define exactly what the function returns, assume it works for the smaller input, and only write the glue: how to combine the small answer into the big one, plus the base case.

sessions.author: Sneha

sessions.author: Priya
sessions.content: Week 3 summary: we covered recursion, subsets, and permutations. Rahul's 'trust the call' trick helped everyone. Next week is dynamic programming. Aman and Sneha want a simple way to see why DP is not just recursion.

sessions.author: Aman
sessions.content: If DP is just recursion, why is it faster? Fibonacci recursion takes forever for n=40 but people say DP solves it instantly.

sessions.author: Rahul
sessions.content: Think of DP as filling a table so you never solve the same subproblem twice. Plain recursion is like re-doing the same homework question every time it shows up. DP writes the answer in a notebook the first time. Ask two things: what is the state (the notebook's row and column), and what earlier cells does a new cell depend on.

sessions.author: Priya
sessions.content: Memoization is top-down and lazy: recurse, and cache answers as you return. Tabulation is bottom-up and eager: fill the table from the smallest case up. Same idea. Use memoization when you only need some states, tabulation when you need all of them or want to avoid recursion depth limits.

sessions.author: Aman
sessions.content: Scored 3/5 on the DP quiz. Got the 0/1 knapsack wrong: I looped over capacity from small to large in the 1D array, so items got reused like unbounded knapsack.

sessions.author: Rahul
sessions.content: Session recap: we did coin change and climbing stairs with tabulation. Reminder from the knapsack mistake: in 1D 0/1 knapsack, loop capacity from high to low so each item is used once. Looping low to high turns it into unbounded knapsack.

sessions.author: Priya
sessions.content: BFS is ripples in a pond: it explores everything one step away, then two steps away, so it finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. DFS is walking a maze until you hit a wall, then backing up. Use BFS for shortest path, DFS for exploring, cycles, and ordering problems.

sessions.author: Aman
sessions.content: When exactly do I need a visited set in DFS or BFS? In trees I never needed one but in graphs my code loops forever.

sessions.author: Rahul
sessions.content: Topological sort is course scheduling. Take any course with zero remaining prerequisites, then cross it off every other course's list. Repeat. That is Kahn's algorithm: keep a queue of nodes with in-degree zero. If you finish and some courses are never taken, the graph has a cycle.

sessions.author: Sneha
sessions.content: Why does Dijkstra fail with negative edges? The heap logic looks fine to me.

sessions.author: Priya
sessions.content: Dijkstra is greedy and makes a promise: once a node is popped from the heap, its distance is final. That is only safe if no later path can be shorter, which breaks the moment a negative edge exists. For negative edges use Bellman-Ford.

sessions.author: Sneha
sessions.content: For top-k largest elements, why use a heap instead of just sorting? Sorting is easier to write.

sessions.author: Rahul
sessions.content: A heap is a tournament bracket where only the current champion on top matters. Sorting ranks everyone, which costs n log n. For top-k, keep a small min-heap of size k: if a new number beats the weakest of your k champions, swap it in. That costs n log k.
